action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active denervation in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles with chronic neurogenic change in bulbar, cervical and lumbosacral muscles, normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block, and mildly reduced sural responses with normal upper limb sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral corticospinal tract T2/FLAIR hyperintensity (supportive only) and mild age-appropriate small vessel change; no mass, haemorrhage, infarct or demyelinating lesion.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs, including vascular lesions in a patient with diabetes and hypertension; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No cervical or thoracic cord compression, cord signal abnormality or mass.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 820 U/L (4.7x ULN) and a mildly raised glucose in known diabetes; normal blood count, renal and liver function, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic: here vitamin B12 matters because long-term metformin can lower it.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 78% predicted and SNIP 62 cmH2O, both reduced, without an AAN 2009 NIV marker.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansion and no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS or TBK1.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Metformin and lisinopril need no change; transaminases are checked before the first dose and on schedule, with riluzole stopped if ALT exceeds 5x ULN.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. No current medicine interacts with it.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not wait for FVC to fall below 50% or for respiratory symptoms before referring for NIV assessment.
Do not attribute the weakness, wasting and bulbar signs to diabetic neuropathy or diabetic amyotrophy: they do not cause upper motor neuron signs or tongue denervation.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive limb weakness with bulbar involvement, with upper motor neuron signs (brisk jaw jerk, brisk reflexes, bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs, spastic gait) and lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar, cervical and lumbosacral regions on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family, explaining that the mild diabetic neuropathy is a separate, coexisting condition.

Refer to the respiratory/NIV service now because FVC (78% predicted) and SNIP (62 cmH2O) are already reduced; screen for orthopnoea and nocturnal hypoventilation with overnight oximetry or capnography, and repeat FVC and SNIP within 3 months.
Arrange a speech and language therapy assessment of speech and swallowing, with communication support, and monitor weight and swallowing at each review.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

accepted: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) with concurrent mild diabetic neuropathy

differential.key_features: supports: type 2 diabetes, leg weakness and wasting; against: symmetric weakness of arms and legs, tongue atrophy and fasciculations, upper motor neuron signs (brisk jaw jerk, Hoffman and Babinski signs, spastic gait) and denervation in bulbar, cervical and thoracic muscles

against: upper motor neuron signs, normal motor conduction velocities and no conduction block, bulbar involvement

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: brisk jaw jerk, brisk reflexes, bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs and spastic gait with lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar, cervical and lumbosacral regions, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.

Mildly reduced sural responses fit a coexisting length-dependent neuropathy, here diabetic, and do not explain widespread motor denervation; motor conduction velocities are normal with no conduction block.
CK 820 U/L (4.7x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

FVC 78% predicted and SNIP 62 cmH2O are already reduced, without an AAN 2009 NIV marker yet. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The coexisting diabetic neuropathy explains the mildly reduced sural responses and toe vibration loss, but not the weakness, wasting, tongue denervation, upper motor neuron signs or the widespread motor denervation with normal motor conduction velocities.
red_herrings.data_point: Mildly reduced sural sensory responses and toe vibration loss from diabetic neuropathy
red_herrings.intended_effect: Confuses the ALS picture with a diabetic sensorimotor neuropathy or diabetic amyotrophy

sequence_constraints.reason: Genetic testing follows the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment and pre-test counselling; it does not make the diagnosis.
Riluzole is considered only after the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment supports ALS.

findings.finding: Tongue: fibrillation potentials 1+ and fasciculation potentials; large, long-duration motor unit potentials with reduced recruitment.
Bilateral first dorsal interosseous: fibrillation potentials 2+, large, long-duration motor unit potentials with reduced recruitment. Cervical paraspinals: fibrillation potentials 1+.
Bilateral tibialis anterior: fibrillation potentials 1+, large, long-duration motor unit potentials with reduced recruitment. Gastrocnemii: fasciculation potentials.
Median, ulnar, peroneal and tibial motor studies: CMAP amplitudes reduced in the wasted muscles, distal latencies and conduction velocities normal, no conduction block and no temporal dispersion.
Sural sensory responses mildly reduced in amplitude bilaterally with normal conduction velocity. Median and ulnar sensory responses normal.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Active denervation in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles, with chronic neurogenic change in bulbar, cervical and lumbosacral muscles and fasciculation potentials in the tongue and gastrocnemii. 2. Reduced CMAP amplitudes with normal distal latencies and conduction velocities; no conduction block. 3. Mildly reduced sural sensory responses bilaterally with normal upper limb sensory studies, consistent with a mild length-dependent sensory neuropathy. The motor findings indicate a widespread disorder of anterior horn cells, consistent with a motor neuron disease; the sural changes are a separate length-dependent process.
